exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $S$ be the set of all polynomials in the real variable $x$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}.$ Complete the following sentence:

$S$ is not a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because $\textrm{_________}\,.$
question.choice1: multiplication of functions in  $S$ by real scalars is not closed
question.choice2: addition of polynomials is not associative
question.choice3: addition of polynomials is not commutative
question.choice4: $S$ does not contain the zero function
question.explanation:
The correct answer is as follows:

$S$ is not a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because multiplication of functions in $S$ by real scalars is not closed.

Indeed, let's consider, for example, the polynomial $f(x) =x.$ Then $f\in S$, but $\sqrt2f(x)= \sqrt2 \! \ x\notin S$ because $\sqrt2 \notin \Bbb Q.$ On the other hand:

  • Addition of polynomials is associative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition of polynomials is commutative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • The zero function belongs to $S.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • $1\cdot f = f$ for all $f \in S.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

example.title: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $J$ be the set of purely imaginary complex numbers, that is, complex numbers of the form $a \mathrm i, $ where $a$ is a nonzero real number. Complete the following sentence:

$J$ is not a vector space (with respect to addition of complex numbers and scalar multiplication of a complex number by a real number) because $\textrm{_________}\,.$
question.choice1: multiplication of $z\in J$ by real  scalars is not closed
question.choice4: Addition and scalar multiplication in $J$ satisfy the distributive laws
question.choice5: $J$ does not contain the element $-z$ for every $z \in J$
question.explanation:
The correct answer is as follows:

$J$ is not a vector space (with respect to addition of complex numbers and scalar multiplication of a complex number by a real number) because multiplication of $z\in J$ by real scalars is not closed.

For example, if $\alpha=0$ and $z=\mathrm i, $ then $\alpha\cdot z = 0\cdot \mathrm i =0 \notin J. $

On the other hand:

  • Addition in $J$ is associative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition in $J$ is commutative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition and scalar multiplication in $J$ satisfy the distributive laws. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • If $z\in J$ then $z=a\mathrm i$ for some $a\in \Bbb R. $ Hence, $-z = (-a)\mathrm i \in J $ since $ -a \in \Bbb R.$ $\, {\color{green}\checkmark}$

example.title: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $U$ be the set of functions $f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(0) = 1.$ Complete the following sentence:

$U$ is not a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication of a function by a real number) because $\textrm{_________}\,.$
question.choice1: multiplication of $f\in U$ by a scalar is not closed
question.choice2: addition of functions is not associative
question.choice3: addition of functions is not commutative
question.choice4: addition and scalar multiplication of polynomials do not satisfy the distributive laws
question.choice5: $U$ does not contain the constant function $ f ( x )=1$  for every $x\in \Bbb R$
question.explanation:
The correct answer is as follows:

$U$ is not a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication of a function by a real number) because multiplication of $f\in U$ by a scalar is not closed.

For example, if $\alpha=2$ and $f(x)=x+1,$ then $f(x)\in U$ but $\alpha f(x) \notin U .$ Indeed, we have that $f(0)=1$ and $2f(0)=2.$

On the other hand:

  • Addition of functions is associative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition of functions is commutative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition and scalar multiplication of functions satisfy the distributive laws. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • The constant function $ f ( x )=1$ for every $x\in \Bbb R$, satisfies $f(0)=1.$ Thus, it is an element of $U.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

example.title: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $Y$ be the set of all polynomials in the variable $x\in \mathbb R$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{R}$ of degree exactly $2.$ Complete the following sentence:

$Y$ is not a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because $\textrm{_________}\,.$
question.choice1: addition of polynomials in $Y$ is not closed
question.choice3: addition and scalar multiplication of polynomials do not satisfy the distributive laws
question.choice4: addition of polynomials is not commutative
question.choice5: addition of polynomials is not associative
question.explanation:
The correct answer is as follows:

$Y$ is not a vector space (with respect to polynomials addition and multiplication of a polynomial by a real number) because addition of polynomials in $Y$ is not closed.

Indeed, let's consider, for example, the polynomials $p(x) = x^2+x$ and $q(x) = -x^2.$ Then $p,q \in Y,$ but \[ p(x)+q(x) = x^2+x + (-x^2) = x \notin Y\] because $\deg(p+q) = 1 \neq 2.$

On the other hand:

  • $1 \cdot p = p$ for all $p \in Y.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition and scalar multiplication of polynomials satisfy the distributive laws. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition of polynomials is commutative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Addition of polynomials is associative. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

example.title: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

question.text:
Let $Z$ be the set of all $2 \times 2$ matrices with real entries and determinant $0.$ Complete the following sentence:

$Z$ is not a vector space (with respect to addition of matrices and multiplication of a matrix by a real number) because $\textrm{____}\,.$
question.choice1: addition of matrices in $Z$ is not closed
question.choice2: $Z$ does not contain the zero matrix $\mathbf{O}$
question.choice3: there exists a matrix $A \in Z$ such that $A+B \neq \mathbf{O}$ for any $B \in Z$
question.choice4: multiplication by a scalar is not closed
question.choice5: multiplication by a scalar is not associative
question.explanation:
The correct answer is

$Z$ is not a vector space (with respect to addition of matrices and multiplication of a matrix by a real number) because addition of matrices in $Z$ is not closed.

For example, consider the matrices $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} $ and $ B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $ in $Z.$ Then, \[ \det(A+B) = \det\left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) = \left| \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right| =1 \neq 0. \] Hence, $A+B \notin Z.$

On the other hand,

  • The zero matrix belongs to $Z.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Given any $A \in Z,$ the additive inverse matrix $-A=(-1)\cdot A$ is also in $Z$ since $\det(-A) = (-1)^2 \cdot \det(A) = 1 \cdot 0 = 0,$ and $A+(-A) = \mathbf{O}.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Given any $A \in Z,$ multiplication by a scalar $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ is closed since $\det(\alpha A) = \alpha^2 \cdot \det(A) = \alpha^2 \cdot 0 = 0.$ Hence, $\alpha A \in Z.$ $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • Multiplication of matrices with real entries by a scalar is associative, in general. $\:{\color{green}\checkmark}$

exampleAnswers.title: Proving Statements Using the Vector Space Axioms

question.text:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

Statement:

If $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ are vectors such that $\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{z} + \mathbf{x}$ for some $\mathbf{x}\in V$, then $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{z}.$

Proof: \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{z}+\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\mathbf{x}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] (\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{axiom A1}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{y}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) &= \mathbf{z}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{z}+\mathbf{0}&& [\:\textrm{axiom A4}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{y} &=\mathbf{z} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \end{align*}

The axioms: \[ \begin{array}{ll} {\color{black}\textrm{[A1]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A5]}}: {\color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A2]}}: {\color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A6]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A3]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A7]}}: {\color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A4]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A8]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}} \end{array} \]
question.explanation:
Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{z}+\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\mathbf{x}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] (\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{axiom A1}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{y}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) &= \mathbf{z}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) && [\,\text{axiom }{\color{blue}{\textrm{A2}}}\,] \\[3pt] \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{z}+\mathbf{0}&& [\:\textrm{axiom A4}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{y} &=\mathbf{z} && [\,\text{axiom }{\color{blue}{\textrm{A3}}}\,] \end{align*}

question.text:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

Statement:

$0 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$

Proof: \begin{align*} 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} && [\:\text{given}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} + 1\cdot\mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom A5}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= (0+1) \cdot \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{addition of integers}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \end{align*}

The axioms: \[ \begin{array}{ll} {\color{black}\textrm{[A1]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A5]}}: {\color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A2]}}: {\color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A6]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A3]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A7]}}: {\color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A4]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A8]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}} \end{array} \]
question.explanation:
Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} && [\:\text{given}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} + 1\cdot\mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom A5}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= (0+1) \cdot \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom $\color{blue}\textrm{A7}$}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{addition of integers}\:] \\[3pt] 0 \cdot \mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom $\color{blue}\textrm{A5}$}\:] \end{align*}

question.text:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

Statement:

If $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are vectors such that $\mathbf x+ \mathbf u =\mathbf x + \mathbf v$ for some $\mathbf x \in V,$ then $\mathbf u = \mathbf v.$

Proof: \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{u} &= \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{u})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\mathbf{x}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] (\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) &= \mathbf{v}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{0}&& [\:\textrm{axiom A4}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{u} &=\mathbf{v} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:] \end{align*}

The axioms: \[ \begin{array}{ll} {\color{black}\textrm{[A1]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A5]}}: {\color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A2]}}: {\color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A6]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A3]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A7]}}: {\color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A4]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A8]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}} \end{array} \]
question.explanation:
Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{u} &= \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{u})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{v})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\mathbf{x}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] (\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\,\text{axiom }{\color{blue}{\textrm{A1}}}\,] \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) &= \mathbf{v}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) && [\,\text{axiom }{\color{blue}{\textrm{A2}}}\,] \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{0}&& [\:\textrm{axiom A4}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{u} &=\mathbf{v} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:] \end{align*}

question.text:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

Statement:

$\alpha\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$ for any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$

Proof: \begin{align*} \alpha\mathbf{0} &= \alpha\mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha\mathbf{0} &= \alpha( \mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0}) && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha \mathbf{0} &= \alpha \mathbf{0}+\alpha\mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \\[3pt] \alpha\mathbf{0}+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}) &=(\alpha\mathbf{0}+\alpha\mathbf{0})+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\alpha\mathbf{0}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha\mathbf{0}+(-\alpha\mathbf{0} )&=\alpha\mathbf{0}+(\alpha\mathbf{0}+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}))&& [\:\textrm{axiom A2}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{0} &= \alpha\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0}&& [\:\textrm{axiom A4}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{0} &=\alpha\mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:\:] \end{align*}

The axioms: \[ \begin{array}{ll} {\color{black}\textrm{[A1]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A5]}}: {\color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A2]}}: {\color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A6]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A3]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A7]}}: {\color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}} \\ {\color{black}\textrm{[A4]}}: {\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}} & {\color{black}\textrm{[A8]}}: {\color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}} \end{array} \]
question.explanation:
Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \alpha\mathbf{0} &= \alpha\mathbf{0} && [\:\text{given}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha\mathbf{0} &= \alpha( \mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0}) && [\:\text{axiom A3}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha \mathbf{0} &= \alpha \mathbf{0}+\alpha\mathbf{0} && [\:\text{axiom }{\color{blue}\text{A8}}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha\mathbf{0}+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}) &=(\alpha\mathbf{0}+\alpha\mathbf{0})+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}) && [\:\text{add }-\alpha\mathbf{0}\text{ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] \alpha\mathbf{0}+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}) &=\alpha\mathbf{0}+(\alpha\mathbf{0}+(-\alpha\mathbf{0}))&& [\:\text{axiom A2}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{0} &= \alpha\mathbf{0}+\mathbf{0}&& [\:\text{axiom A4}\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{0} &=\alpha\mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom }{\color{blue}\text{A3}}\:] \end{align*}

question.text:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

Statement:

Given any $\mathbf{x}\in V$, if $\mathbf{w}$ is a vector such that $\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$, then $\mathbf{w}=-\mathbf{x}$

Proof: \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{w} &= \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{w})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= \mathbf{0}+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\mathbf{x}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{w}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (-\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:]\\[3pt] ( \mathbf{w}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:]\\[3pt] \mathbf{w}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom A2}\:\:]\\[3pt] \mathbf{w}+\mathbf{0} &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom __}\:]\\[3pt] \mathbf{w} &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:\:] \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{w} &= \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{given}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{w})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= \mathbf{0}+(-\mathbf{x}) && [\:\textrm{add $-\mathbf{x}$ to both sides}\:] \\[3pt] ( \mathbf{w}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= (-\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{0} && [\:\textrm{axiom }{\color{blue}A1}\:]\\[3pt] ( \mathbf{w}+\mathbf{x})+(-\mathbf{x}) &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom A3}\:]\\[3pt] \mathbf{w}+(\mathbf{x}+(-\mathbf{x})) &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom $\textrm{A2}$}\:\:] \\[3pt] \mathbf{w}+\mathbf{0} &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom }{ \color{blue}A4}\:]\\[3pt] \mathbf{w} &= -\mathbf{x} && [\:\textrm{axiom $\textrm{A3}$}\:\:] \end{align*}
